title: EU Chief Backs Plan for Canada to Become 'Associate Member'
summary: What if your country could join a club on the other side of the ocean? On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants to 'open the door' for Canada to become the European Union's first 'associate member.' Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was there to listen. Last week, Carney talked about seeking a 'unique alliance' with the EU. Why? Canada is having tense times with the U.S. Trade talks between them collapsed last month, leading to new tariffs (taxes on imports). President Donald Trump has even talked about making Canada the '51st state.' Von der Leyen said the EU and Canada 'see the world with the same eyes' on things like AI, climate change, and defense. She listed areas for cooperation: manufacturing, technology, AI, defense, energy, and critical minerals. But here's the catch: 'associate membership' doesn't exist yet. If agreed, it could take years. Some EU countries would rather build on existing deals than create a new type of membership. Ten of the EU's 27 members haven't even ratified a free-trade agreement with Canada from nearly a decade ago. Carney will speak to the European Parliament on Thursday. The big question: will Canada really get a new seat at Europe's table?
why_it_matters: Countries pick their friends and trading partners carefully, and when old friendships get rocky, new ones can change what kids see in stores and how their countries work together.

background_read: The European Union (a club of 27 European countries that make rules together about trade, travel, and the environment) has only ever had full members — it has never had an 'associate member' before.
Ursula von der Leyen leads the European Commission (the part of the EU that suggests new laws and runs its everyday work), and Mark Carney became Canada's prime minister in 2025.
Canada is a big country just north of the United States and one of its closest trading partners, so when the two argue about tariffs, businesses and shoppers on both sides can feel it.
Article_Structure: WHO: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and the EU's member countries.
WHAT: A plan to make Canada the EU's first-ever 'associate member' — a kind of membership that does not exist yet.
WHERE: Announced in Europe while Canada sits across the Atlantic Ocean; Carney was set to speak to the European Parliament.
WHY: Canada wants a 'unique alliance' because its trade talks with the U.S. fell apart, and the EU wants a closer partner on AI, energy, defense, and critical minerals.

perspectives.description: Von der Leyen says the EU and Canada 'see the world with the same eyes' on AI, climate change, and defense, so a closer partnership makes sense.
